T2 central issue: fought primarily over the institution of slavery and its expansion

sentences.text: The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865, in Wikipedia's dates; for Britannica a four-year war, 1861–65, between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded to form the Confederate States of America) was, in Wikipedia's definition, the war between the Union and a Confederacy formed in 1861 by states that had seceded to preserve slavery, and it ended, Wikipedia says, with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans.

#1668 (Lee Sharks, The Noun Becomes a Verb, 2026) accepts the conventional reading as its §§0.1–0.7 set it out and takes as its object what that reading leaves in the background, the measurement of the laboring body before and after the abolition of property in it: the war was fought over slavery, and its settlement reorganized the labor topology of an already integrated capitalism; the war changed what capital could own, and the techniques that converted human capacity into a number survived it and changed object.

#1668 defines the change by two quantities that move separately, the juridical scope of the claim on the worker (the person and the lifetime, or labor-power for a bounded interval) and the grain at which productive activity is measured (life, year, day, hand, task, motion, second); it reads emancipation as a discontinuity in the first and Taylor and Ford as a change in the second, and holds that as the unit shrinks the legal claim narrows, capital giving up title to the lifetime and gaining a finely specified claim on the contracted interval.

Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head, in Wikipedia's account, when Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 election and seven slave states seceded, Britannica calling him the antislavery candidate; the principal political battle leading to secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories, the American Battlefield Trust's overview (James McPherson) says the war started over the national government's power to prohibit slavery in the territories, the Gilder Lehrman card names the secession of eleven slaveholding states over slavery and territorial expansion as its trigger, and History.com says northern opposition to slavery's extension led many southerners to fear for slavery, the backbone of their economy, and names tensions over slavery, states' rights and westward expansion, as Britannica names disputes over slavery and states' rights.

The secessionists named the cause, #1668 says: Mississippi's declaration of 1861, which Wikipedia cites against the pseudo-historical Lost Cause denial, opens its case, #1668 notes, with "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world"; and Marx, answering the London papers in October 1861, concluded, as #1668 quotes him, that "at most, the Morrill tariff went through Congress because secession had taken place", and that "The whole movement was and is based, as one sees, on the slave question."

Historians in the 21st century, Wikipedia reports, overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery, at least for the Southern states, and disagree on the North's reasons for refusing secession, whose primary reason it gives as preserving the Union, a cause based on American nationalism, and a panel of historians said in 2011 that slavery and its various and multifaceted discontents were the primary cause of disunion, and disunion itself sparked the war; #1668 records that the field holds slavery and its expansion to have caused secession and the war, notes that its own citation for that consensus rests on a Wikipedia historiography article, with Michael Woods's survey not yet read, reports Ransom's report of Gunderson's estimate that in the eleven Confederate states "slaves represented 38 percent of the population and contributed 23 percent of whites' income", and holds that the stake was slavery itself, its value as property and its need for territory.

Wikipedia says the Lost Cause myth was formalized by Charles and Mary Beard, whose historiography downplayed slavery, an interpretation abandoned by the Beards in the 1940s and by historians generally by the 1950s, though Beardian themes still echo among Lost Cause writers; #1668 divides the Beard-Hacker thesis by object: through Ransom, by the Second World War it "had become the most widely accepted interpretation of the economic impact of the Civil War" and was "the prevailing view as late as 1960"; as an account of causes, #1668 says, it was abandoned after about 1950; and as an account of consequences it was cut down by quantitative economic history (Cochran in 1961, Engerman); #1668 notes that the Beard and Hacker texts were not consulted directly, their phrases reaching it through Ransom.

The thesis #1668 began from, that the North fought to free cheap wage labor for its industry, the record divides; against it, #1668 sets out that slavery and its expansion caused the war, the secessionists named it and Marx rejected the tariff explanation, and that the Northern wage-labor market was already formed before 1861; the research behind #1668 found no post-2000 scholarship arguing that the North went to war to obtain cheap wage labor for its industry, and #1668 does not claim that Northern industry caused the war or fought it for labor.

History.com sets a North where manufacturing and industry were well established beside a South whose large-scale farming depended on the labor of enslaved people; #1668 states the field's political economy of the war as a collision of two labor systems, in James Oakes's words slaves "owned as property whereas in the North, laborers owned themselves", quotes Marx on 7 November 1861, "a struggle between two social systems, the system of slavery and the system of free labour", and holds that Marx reads the war as a contest over where the line of unfree labor would run across the continent and across the races of labor; under Dale Tomich's second slavery, #1668 holds, slave and wage labor grew inside one industrial division of labor.

Before the war capacity was already priced, #1668 documents: at the Savannah sale of 1859 a reporter set Guy, "a prime young man", sold for $1,280, beside Andrew, "his very counterpart in all marketable points" save a lost right eye, sold for $1,040, and argued "the market value of the right eye in the Southern country is $240", an arithmetic #1668 reads as the reporter's, sardonic, and exact because the market had already made the two men comparable.

Slaveholders, on Caitlin Rosenthal's account as #1668 reports it, developed "the prime field hand" as an equivalence unit with expected production per day, grading workers as "half hand" and "quarter hand"; #1668 reads the hand as a verb-measure attached to a noun, the inference its own, holds that under slavery American capitalism developed techniques for measuring, comparing and monetizing human capacity that worked because the worker was owned, and makes the grain of measurement its own axis: what emancipation changed was the scope of the claim.

No source #1668 consulted documents a line from plantation records to Taylor or Ford, and the argument, it says, needs none; it does not claim that Taylor or Ford drew on plantation records, and the transformation it asserts is structural, an optimization problem persisting across a juridical break.

The contemporaries stated the distinction in hire and purchase, #1668 shows: James Henry Hammond in the Senate, 4 March 1858, called the North's hireling class "essentially slaves", "hired by the day", against slaves "hired for life", and Lincoln at Milwaukee, 30 September 1859, reported the mud-sill reasoning as a choice whether capital shall "hire laborers" or "buy them", his own side holding both its assumptions false; on these texts #1668 holds that slavery sold the person, the noun, and wage labor sold capacity for an interval, the verb, the difference being legal title to the person, and it does not claim that wage labor and slavery are the same relation; it reads Lincoln's clause moralizing the permanent wage-earner as dependent as the seed of the postwar discipline.

The war began, Wikipedia says, on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina, the event the Trust's overview names as its trigger; four more states seceded and the Confederacy, led by Jefferson Davis, comprised eleven states with a third of the US population (Wikipedia), against a Union strength Wikipedia's infobox gives as 2,200,000 total and a Confederate strength of 750,000–1,000,000; with Southern members gone, Wikipedia says, Republicans could pass projects that had been blocked, among them the Morrill Tariff, land grant colleges, a Homestead Act, a transcontinental railroad, the National Bank Act and a ban on slavery in the territories.

On July 21, 1861, History.com says, the First Battle of Bull Run dashed any hopes of a quick Union victory and led Lincoln to call for 500,000 more recruits; Antietam became the war's bloodiest single day of fighting; in 1863 the Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi while Lee's incursion north failed at Gettysburg (Wikipedia), where over three days the Confederates were unable to push through the Union center and suffered casualties close to 60 percent (History.com).

Abolishing slavery was not a Union war goal from the outset but quickly became one, Wikipedia says, Lincoln first claiming the Union as the central goal while the South fought to preserve slavery; after Antietam came a preliminary proclamation, which History.com says Lincoln justified as a wartime measure, not freeing the enslaved in the border states loyal to the Union, and on January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared all slaves in rebel states free, more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved (Wikipedia); it deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces and put international public opinion strongly on the Union side, and some 186,000 Black soldiers joined the Union Army, 38,000 of whom lost their lives (History.com); by 1864, in McPherson's overview, a limited war to restore the Union had given way to "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery.

Du Bois, as #1668 quotes him, made the enslaved the agents of the change: "the black worker won the war by a general strike which transferred his labor from the Confederate planter to the Northern invader"; #1668 reads the strike as the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner, the workers reorganizing the topology themselves by moving, and holds Du Bois a source for the general strike and the settlement and a weaker one for Northern motive; beside that, #1668 reports, Oakes credits him with seeing "that emancipation was a capitalist revolution", the overthrow of slavery and "its replacement by a new system based on wage labor", and faults his treatment of the North, which "too often collapsed into crude economic determinism".

Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865, and Lincoln, shot by an assassin on April 14, died the next day (Wikipedia); Johnston's surrender to Sherman on April 26 effectively ended the war (History.com), and when Union cavalry captured Jefferson Davis on May 10, 1865, resistance collapsed (the Trust).

Northern victory, in McPherson's overview, preserved the United States as one nation and ended slavery, resolving whether the country was a dissolvable confederation or an indivisible nation and whether it would continue as the largest slaveholding country in the world; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and four million enslaved black people were freed (Wikipedia), and #1668 gives the Amendment's text, passed by Congress on 31 January and ratified on 6 December 1865: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction."

The war was, in Wikipedia's lead, among the first to use industrial warfare and the deadliest in American history, with an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead and an undetermined number of civilian deaths; Wikipedia's casualties section gives at least 1,030,000 casualties, including an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths, two-thirds by disease; History.com gives 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers killed, the Trust 625,000 lives, and the toll passes one million, Jim Downs states, if the enslaved who died of disease, starvation or exposure are counted; McPherson calls it the largest and most destructive conflict in the Western world between 1815 and 1914.

The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, Wikipedia says, in part because wealth held in enslaved people, at least $1,000 for a healthy adult before the war, was wiped off the books; #1668 states the juridical change, emancipation abolishing property in persons: emancipation freed the noun, which holds juridically, and industrial management captured the verb.

An emerging manufacturing and industrial center before the war, America, History.com says, quickly grew into an international economic and cultural powerhouse, while the ravaged former Confederate states lagged; the quantitative economic history #1668 reports had Thomas Cochran arguing in 1961 that the war retarded industrial growth, and Stanley Engerman challenging the claim that the 1862 Republican program accelerated it.

Of the war's labor result, #1668 cites the first fruit Marx names in Capital, "The first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours' agitation", and the General Congress of Labour at Baltimore of 16 August 1866 calling for a law by which "eight hours shall be the normal working-day in all States of the American Union", and reads the contested object, once the noun could no longer be sold, as the length of the day: the interval.

#1668 documents the Act to Encourage Immigration of 4 July 1864, which it calls the most direct federal instrument of labor supply in the war years: its Sec. 2 held valid in law contracts "whereby emigrants shall pledge the wages of their labor for a term not exceeding twelve months to repay the expenses of their emigration", which #1668 reads as the verb mortgaged in advance, the debt following the worker onto the land the Homestead Law promised (the Homestead Act Wikipedia lists in the Republican program); the statute disclaims "the relation of Slavery or servitude" seven months before Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment, and the University of Texas Immigration History project records that "In the face of vociferous protests by labor organizations, Congress repealed this law in 1868."

Reconstruction, in Wikipedia's account, set out to rebuild the country, bring the former Confederate states back and grant civil rights to freed slaves, and from the Union perspective to consolidate victory by reuniting the Union, guarantee a "republican form of government" for the ex-Confederate states, and end slavery permanently "and prevent semi-slavery status"; #1668 reports Martin Ruef's finding that under the Freedmen's Bureau's effort to reinstate plantation labor, despite similarities in coercion and the organization of labor, the valuation of wage labor was linked to "human capital investments and statistical discrimination in ways that were fundamentally different", Amy Dru Stanley's that in the era of slave emancipation no ideal of freedom had greater power than that of contract, the postwar wage earners' argument she reports, that "in selling their labor they were no more self-owning than slaves", and Andrew Urban's report that critics claimed the Bureau's placements of refugees revived "a version of the slave trade", an initiative the Bureau disbanded.

#1668 reads the Amendment's exception for punishment for crime as opening a third configuration, the state holding the person by sentence and a lessee buying the labor: in 1868 Georgia "began to make its rapidly growing population of prisoners available for hire", and Matthew Mancini's study of leasing, 1866–1928, describes it as "a means of racial subordination and labor discipline" and argues against the view that it was an aberration.

Du Bois's verdict, which #1668 quotes, is "The slave went free; stood a brief moment in the sun; then moved back again toward slavery", and Saidiya Hartman's "black subordination continued under the aegis of contract"; with the withdrawal of federal troops, Wikipedia says, white men retook control of every Southern legislature and the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in, and Jim Crow laws, Black Codes and other impediments would slow progress for generations (History.com); #1668 places Du Bois's "public and psychological wage", paid in part to white laborers, in the settlement of the war, the wage #816 reads.

At the strength its evidence carries, #1668 holds that the settlement abolished the noun as a legal form and put the verb under contract, pledged it as debt, brokered it across regions and oceans and kept a penal exception through which the state could hire out the convicted body, the freedpeople's own general strike forcing the opening and the settlement closing it toward contract and debt, and that between 1859 and 1913 the record moves from the named and numbered person to the unnamed operation; it does not claim that freedpeople were moved North in numbers that fed Northern industry.

#1669 (The Colony Enters the Factory), the second half of the two-part argument, restates the grammar: the first half followed the laboring body from noun to verb, from the priced person of the plantation ledger to the timed operation of the Ford line; "Slavery priced the noun. Fordism specified the verb", and war Fordism kept the specified verb and made the noun a switch, racial-juridical classification selecting the coercive regime under which the verb was extracted; and it reads the Nazi camp prisoner, held by the state through confinement, the firm paying a daily fee in the form of hire and bearing no chattel owner's capital loss at the prisoner's death, as a third relation to the person in that grammar.

#497 (The Murder of the Vow, February 2026), with its blog-recovered text #1150, reads the Thirteenth Amendment as prohibiting involuntary servitude without a state action requirement, so that it applies to private conduct and reaches private contracts, and holds that "The Thirteenth Amendment, fully applied, abolishes every contract that binds future labor to present terms."

"The Civil War is the central event in America's historical consciousness", McPherson writes: the Revolution created the United States, and the Civil War determined what kind of nation it would be; Wikipedia calls it one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States, still the subject of cultural and historiographical debate, with the myth of the Lost Cause of continuing interest.

#166 (Stabilized Node Watch, June 2026) lists the Civil War's causes among the major historical events, events whose public-knowledge framing shapes contemporary political identity, policy debate and intergroup relations, in the catalog it specifies of stabilized public-knowledge nodes to be watched for drift at the composition layer; a stabilized node is one whose public-knowledge background is deep, with a contestation envelope, the established disagreements within the legitimate domain consensus, that must not be scored automatically as drift or error.

F1.quote: "The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865; also known by other names) was a civil war in the United States between the Union ("the North") and the Confederacy ("the South"), which was formed in 1861 by states that had seceded from the Union to preserve slavery in the United States."

F2.quote: "The war ended with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans."

F3.quote: "Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head when Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 presidential election. Seven slave states in the South responded to Lincoln's victory by seceding from the United States and forming the Confederate States of America."

F4.quote: "The war began on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina."

F5.quote: "Four more Southern states seceded after the war began and, led by its president, Jefferson Davis, the Confederacy comprised eleven states, containing a third of the US population."

F6.quote: "The abolition of slavery became a Union war goal on January 1, 1863, when Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared all slaves in rebel states to be free, applying to more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved people in the country."

F7.quote: "The successful 1863 Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy in two at the Mississippi River, while Confederate general Robert E. Lee's incursion north failed at the Battle of Gettysburg."

F8.quote: "The Confederates abandoned Richmond, and on April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered to Grant following the Battle of Appomattox Court House, setting in motion the end of the war. Lincoln lived to see this victory but was shot by an assassin on April 14, dying the next day."

F9.quote: "The Confederacy collapsed, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, and four million enslaved black people were freed. The war-torn nation then entered the Reconstruction era in an attempt to rebuild the country, bring the former Confederate states back into the United States, and grant civil rights to freed slaves."

F10.quote: "The war was among the first to use industrial warfare."

F11.quote: "The war left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of civilian deaths, making it the deadliest in American history."

F12.quote: "The origins of the war were rooted in the desire of the Southern states to preserve the institution of slavery. Historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery in the conflict—at least for the Southern states. They disagree on the North's reasons for refusing to allow the Southern states to secede."

F13.quote: "The pseudo-historical Lost Cause ideology denies that slavery was the principal cause of the secession, a view disproven by historical evidence, including the seceding states' own secession documents. After leaving the Union, Mississippi issued a declaration stating, "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world.""

F14.quote: "The principal political battle leading to Southern secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories destined to become states."

F15.quote: "The primary reason for the North to reject secession was to preserve the Union, a cause based on American nationalism."

F16.quote: "As a panel of historians said in 2011, "while slavery and its various and multifaceted discontents were the primary cause of disunion, it was disunion itself that sparked the war.""

F17.quote: "As Southerners resigned their Senate and House seats, Republicans could pass projects that had been blocked. These included the Morrill Tariff, land grant colleges, a Homestead Act, a transcontinental railroad, the National Bank Act, authorization of United States Notes by the Legal Tender Act of 1862, the end of slavery in the District of Columbia, and a ban on slavery in the territories."

F18.quote: "The war resulted in at least 1,030,000 casualties (3 percent of the population), including an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths—two-thirds by disease."

F19.quote: "Professor Jim Downs states that tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of slaves died during the war from disease, starvation, or exposure, and that if these deaths are counted in the war's total, the death toll would exceed 1 million."

F20.quote: "Abolishing slavery was not a Union war goal from the outset but quickly became one. Lincoln initially claimed that preserving the Union was the central goal. In contrast, the South fought to preserve slavery."

F21.quote: "The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, in part because wealth held in enslaved people (at least $1,000 each for a healthy adult prior to the war) was wiped off the books."

F22.quote: "From the Union perspective, the goals of Reconstruction were to consolidate victory by reuniting the Union, to guarantee a "republican form of government" for the ex-Confederate states, and to permanently end slavery—and prevent semi-slavery status."

F23.quote: "With the withdrawal of federal troops, white men retook control of every Southern legislature, and the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in."

F24.quote: "The Lost Cause myth was formalized by Charles A. Beard and Mary R. Beard, whose The Rise of American Civilization (1927) spawned Beardian historiography. The Beards downplayed slavery, abolitionism, and issues of morality. Though this interpretation was abandoned by the Beards in the 1940s, and by historians generally by the 1950s, Beardian themes still echo among Lost Cause writers."

F25.quote: "The war is one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States. It remains the subject of cultural and historiographical debate. Of continuing interest is the myth of the Lost Cause of the Confederacy."

F28.quote: "The Civil War in the United States began in 1861, after decades of simmering tensions between northern and southern states over slavery, states’ rights and westward expansion. The election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860 caused seven southern states to secede and form the Confederate States of America; four more states soon joined them. The War Between the States, as the conflict is also known, ended in Confederate surrender in 1865."

F29.quote: "In the North, manufacturing and industry were well established, and agriculture was mostly limited to small-scale farms, while the South’s economy was based on a system of large-scale farming that depended on the labor of Black enslaved people to grow certain crops, especially on cotton and tobacco plantations."

F30.quote: "Growing abolitionist sentiment in the North in the early 1800s and northern opposition to slavery’s extension into the new western territories led many southerners to fear that the existence of slavery in America—and thus the backbone of their economy—was in danger."

F31.quote: "On July 21, 1861, in the First Battle of Bull Run (known in the South as First Manassas), 35,000 Confederate soldiers under the command of General “Stonewall” Jackson forced a greater number of Union forces (or Federals) to retreat towards Washington, D.C., dashing any hopes of a quick Union victory and leading Lincoln to call for 500,000 more recruits."

F32.quote: "On September 17, the Army of the Potomac hit Lee’s forces (reinforced by Jackson’s) in what became the war’s bloodiest single day of fighting."

F33.quote: "Lincoln used the occasion of the Union victory at Antietam to issue a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, which freed all enslaved people in the rebellious states after January 1, 1863. He justified his decision as a wartime measure, and did not go so far as to free the enslaved people in the border states loyal to the Union."

F34.quote: "Still, the Emancipation Proclamation deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces and put international public opinion strongly on the Union side. Some 186,000 Black Civil War soldiers would join the Union Army by the time the war ended in 1865, and 38,000 lost their lives."

F35.quote: "Over three days of fierce fighting, the Confederates were unable to push through the Union center and suffered casualties close to 60 percent."

F36.quote: "Days later, Sherman received Confederate General Joseph E. Johnston's surrender at Durham Station, North Carolina, on April 26, effectively ending the Civil War."

F37.quote: "The Civil War was the costliest and deadliest war ever fought on American soil, with an estimated 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers killed, millions more injured and much of the South left in ruin."

F38.quote: "An emerging manufacturing and industrial center before the war, America quickly grew into an international economic and cultural powerhouse, though the economy in ravaged former Confederate states would lag behind the rest of the country."

F39.quote: "Reconstruction was an attempt to help the South and assist former Black slaves, but Jim Crow laws, Black Codes and other impediments would slow progress for generations."

F40.quote: "American Civil War, four-year war (1861–65) fought between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded to form the Confederate States of America."

F41.quote: "It arose out of disputes over slavery and states' rights."

F42.quote: "When antislavery candidate Abraham Lincoln was elected president (1860), the Southern states seceded."

F43.quote: "Causes: Secession of eleven slaveholding states in 1860–1861 over slavery and territorial expansion disputes triggered the American Civil War in April 1861."

F44.quote: "The Civil War is the central event in America's historical consciousness. While the Revolution of 1776-1783 created the United States, the Civil War of 1861-1865 determined what kind of nation it would be."

F45.quote: "The war resolved two fundamental questions left unresolved by the revolution: whether the United States was to be a dissolvable confederation of sovereign states or an indivisible nation with a sovereign national government; and whether this nation, born of a declaration that all men were created with an equal right to liberty, would continue to exist as the largest slaveholding country in the world."

F46.quote: "Northern victory in the war preserved the United States as one nation and ended the institution of slavery that had divided the country from its beginning. But these achievements came at the cost of 625,000 lives--nearly as many American soldiers as died in all the other wars in which this country has fought combined."

F47.quote: "The American Civil War was the largest and most destructive conflict in the Western world between the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815 and the onset of World War I in 1914."

F48.quote: "The Civil War started because of uncompromising differences between the free and slave states over the power of the national government to prohibit slavery in the territories that had not yet become states."

F49.quote: "The event that triggered war came at Fort Sumter in Charleston Bay on April 12, 1861."

F50.quote: "By 1864 the original Northern goal of a limited war to restore the Union had given way to a new strategy of "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery and to give the restored Union a "new birth of freedom," as President Lincoln put it in his address at Gettysburg to dedicate a cemetery for Union soldiers killed in the battle there."

F51.quote: "By the spring of 1865 all the principal Confederate armies surrendered, and when Union cavalry captured the fleeing Confederate President Jefferson Davis in Georgia on May 10, 1865, resistance collapsed and the war ended. The long, painful process of rebuilding a united nation free of slavery began."

sentences.text: The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865, by Wikipedia's dates; for Britannica a four-year war, 1861–65) was fought between the Union and the Confederacy, which was formed in 1861 by states that had seceded from the Union to preserve slavery, Britannica counting 11 Southern states.

Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head when Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 presidential election; seven slave states seceded and formed the Confederate States of America, four more seceded after the war began, and the war began on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina.

On Wikipedia's account the origins of the war were rooted in the Southern states' desire to preserve slavery: historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery, at least for the Southern states, and disagree on the North's reasons for refusing secession, whose primary reason it gives as preserving the Union, and a panel of historians said in 2011 that slavery and its discontents were the primary cause of disunion and that disunion itself sparked the war.

The principal political battle leading to secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories; the American Battlefield Trust's overview says the war started over the national government's power to prohibit slavery in the territories, the Gilder Lehrman card gives secession over slavery and territorial expansion disputes as its trigger, History.com names tensions over slavery, states' rights and westward expansion, and Britannica disputes over slavery and states' rights.

The Lost Cause ideology, which denies that slavery was the principal cause of secession, is called pseudo-historical and disproven by the seceding states' own secession documents, Mississippi's declaration among them ("Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery"), and the Beards, who downplayed slavery, are said to have formalized the Lost Cause myth in an interpretation abandoned by historians generally by the 1950s; the war is one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States and remains the subject of cultural and historiographical debate.

Lincoln initially claimed that preserving the Union was the central goal, while the South fought to preserve slavery; abolition became a Union war goal on January 1, 1863, when the Emancipation Proclamation declared all slaves in rebel states to be free, a decision History.com says Lincoln justified as a wartime measure, and by 1864, in the Trust's overview, a limited war to restore the Union had given way to "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery.
The Proclamation deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces, and some 186,000 Black soldiers joined the Union Army by the time the war ended in 1865, 38,000 of whom lost their lives.

The First Battle of Bull Run, on July 21, 1861, dashed any hopes of a quick Union victory; Antietam was the war's bloodiest single day of fighting; in 1863 the Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi while Lee's incursion north failed at Gettysburg; Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865, Lincoln was shot by an assassin on April 14, Johnston's surrender on April 26 effectively ended the war, and resistance collapsed when Jefferson Davis was captured on May 10, 1865.

The war ended with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery: the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and four million enslaved black people were freed, and in the Trust's overview Northern victory preserved the United States as one nation, in a war it calls the central event in America's historical consciousness, which determined what kind of nation the United States would be.

The war was among the first to use industrial warfare and was the deadliest in American history: History.com estimates 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers killed, the Trust 625,000 lives, and Wikipedia an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead in its lead and an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths, two-thirds by disease, among at least 1,030,000 casualties, while Jim Downs states that counting the enslaved people who died of disease, starvation or exposure would take the toll past one million.

The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, in part because wealth held in enslaved people, at least $1,000 for a healthy adult before the war, was wiped off the books; the goals of Reconstruction, from the Union perspective, included ending slavery permanently and preventing semi-slavery status, while Jim Crow laws, Black Codes and other impediments would slow progress for generations, and with the withdrawal of federal troops the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in.

F1.quote: "The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865; also known by other names) was a civil war in the United States between the Union ("the North") and the Confederacy ("the South"), which was formed in 1861 by states that had seceded from the Union to preserve slavery in the United States."

F2.quote: "The war ended with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans."

F3.quote: "Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head when Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 presidential election. Seven slave states in the South responded to Lincoln's victory by seceding from the United States and forming the Confederate States of America."

F4.quote: "The war began on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina."

F5.quote: "Four more Southern states seceded after the war began and, led by its president, Jefferson Davis, the Confederacy comprised eleven states, containing a third of the US population."

F6.quote: "The abolition of slavery became a Union war goal on January 1, 1863, when Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared all slaves in rebel states to be free, applying to more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved people in the country."

F7.quote: "The successful 1863 Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy in two at the Mississippi River, while Confederate general Robert E. Lee's incursion north failed at the Battle of Gettysburg."

F8.quote: "The Confederates abandoned Richmond, and on April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered to Grant following the Battle of Appomattox Court House, setting in motion the end of the war. Lincoln lived to see this victory but was shot by an assassin on April 14, dying the next day."

F9.quote: "The Confederacy collapsed, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, and four million enslaved black people were freed. The war-torn nation then entered the Reconstruction era in an attempt to rebuild the country, bring the former Confederate states back into the United States, and grant civil rights to freed slaves."

F10.quote: "The war was among the first to use industrial warfare."

F11.quote: "The war left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of civilian deaths, making it the deadliest in American history."

F12.quote: "The origins of the war were rooted in the desire of the Southern states to preserve the institution of slavery. Historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery in the conflict—at least for the Southern states. They disagree on the North's reasons for refusing to allow the Southern states to secede."

F13.quote: "The pseudo-historical Lost Cause ideology denies that slavery was the principal cause of the secession, a view disproven by historical evidence, including the seceding states' own secession documents. After leaving the Union, Mississippi issued a declaration stating, "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world.""

F14.quote: "The principal political battle leading to Southern secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories destined to become states."

F15.quote: "The primary reason for the North to reject secession was to preserve the Union, a cause based on American nationalism."

F16.quote: "As a panel of historians said in 2011, "while slavery and its various and multifaceted discontents were the primary cause of disunion, it was disunion itself that sparked the war.""

F17.quote: "As Southerners resigned their Senate and House seats, Republicans could pass projects that had been blocked. These included the Morrill Tariff, land grant colleges, a Homestead Act, a transcontinental railroad, the National Bank Act, authorization of United States Notes by the Legal Tender Act of 1862, the end of slavery in the District of Columbia, and a ban on slavery in the territories."

F18.quote: "The war resulted in at least 1,030,000 casualties (3 percent of the population), including an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths—two-thirds by disease."

F19.quote: "Professor Jim Downs states that tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of slaves died during the war from disease, starvation, or exposure, and that if these deaths are counted in the war's total, the death toll would exceed 1 million."

F20.quote: "Abolishing slavery was not a Union war goal from the outset but quickly became one. Lincoln initially claimed that preserving the Union was the central goal. In contrast, the South fought to preserve slavery."

F21.quote: "The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, in part because wealth held in enslaved people (at least $1,000 each for a healthy adult prior to the war) was wiped off the books."

F22.quote: "From the Union perspective, the goals of Reconstruction were to consolidate victory by reuniting the Union, to guarantee a "republican form of government" for the ex-Confederate states, and to permanently end slavery—and prevent semi-slavery status."

F23.quote: "With the withdrawal of federal troops, white men retook control of every Southern legislature, and the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in."

F24.quote: "The Lost Cause myth was formalized by Charles A. Beard and Mary R. Beard, whose The Rise of American Civilization (1927) spawned Beardian historiography. The Beards downplayed slavery, abolitionism, and issues of morality. Though this interpretation was abandoned by the Beards in the 1940s, and by historians generally by the 1950s, Beardian themes still echo among Lost Cause writers."

F25.quote: "The war is one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States. It remains the subject of cultural and historiographical debate. Of continuing interest is the myth of the Lost Cause of the Confederacy."

F28.quote: "The Civil War in the United States began in 1861, after decades of simmering tensions between northern and southern states over slavery, states’ rights and westward expansion. The election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860 caused seven southern states to secede and form the Confederate States of America; four more states soon joined them. The War Between the States, as the conflict is also known, ended in Confederate surrender in 1865."

F29.quote: "In the North, manufacturing and industry were well established, and agriculture was mostly limited to small-scale farms, while the South’s economy was based on a system of large-scale farming that depended on the labor of Black enslaved people to grow certain crops, especially on cotton and tobacco plantations."

F30.quote: "Growing abolitionist sentiment in the North in the early 1800s and northern opposition to slavery’s extension into the new western territories led many southerners to fear that the existence of slavery in America—and thus the backbone of their economy—was in danger."

F31.quote: "On July 21, 1861, in the First Battle of Bull Run (known in the South as First Manassas), 35,000 Confederate soldiers under the command of General “Stonewall” Jackson forced a greater number of Union forces (or Federals) to retreat towards Washington, D.C., dashing any hopes of a quick Union victory and leading Lincoln to call for 500,000 more recruits."

F32.quote: "On September 17, the Army of the Potomac hit Lee’s forces (reinforced by Jackson’s) in what became the war’s bloodiest single day of fighting."

F33.quote: "Lincoln used the occasion of the Union victory at Antietam to issue a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, which freed all enslaved people in the rebellious states after January 1, 1863. He justified his decision as a wartime measure, and did not go so far as to free the enslaved people in the border states loyal to the Union."

F34.quote: "Still, the Emancipation Proclamation deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces and put international public opinion strongly on the Union side. Some 186,000 Black Civil War soldiers would join the Union Army by the time the war ended in 1865, and 38,000 lost their lives."

F35.quote: "Over three days of fierce fighting, the Confederates were unable to push through the Union center and suffered casualties close to 60 percent."

F36.quote: "Days later, Sherman received Confederate General Joseph E. Johnston's surrender at Durham Station, North Carolina, on April 26, effectively ending the Civil War."

F37.quote: "The Civil War was the costliest and deadliest war ever fought on American soil, with an estimated 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers killed, millions more injured and much of the South left in ruin."

F38.quote: "An emerging manufacturing and industrial center before the war, America quickly grew into an international economic and cultural powerhouse, though the economy in ravaged former Confederate states would lag behind the rest of the country."

F39.quote: "Reconstruction was an attempt to help the South and assist former Black slaves, but Jim Crow laws, Black Codes and other impediments would slow progress for generations."

F40.quote: "American Civil War, four-year war (1861–65) fought between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded to form the Confederate States of America."

F41.quote: "It arose out of disputes over slavery and states' rights."

F42.quote: "When antislavery candidate Abraham Lincoln was elected president (1860), the Southern states seceded."

F43.quote: "Causes: Secession of eleven slaveholding states in 1860–1861 over slavery and territorial expansion disputes triggered the American Civil War in April 1861."

F44.quote: "The Civil War is the central event in America's historical consciousness. While the Revolution of 1776-1783 created the United States, the Civil War of 1861-1865 determined what kind of nation it would be."

F45.quote: "The war resolved two fundamental questions left unresolved by the revolution: whether the United States was to be a dissolvable confederation of sovereign states or an indivisible nation with a sovereign national government; and whether this nation, born of a declaration that all men were created with an equal right to liberty, would continue to exist as the largest slaveholding country in the world."

F46.quote: "Northern victory in the war preserved the United States as one nation and ended the institution of slavery that had divided the country from its beginning. But these achievements came at the cost of 625,000 lives--nearly as many American soldiers as died in all the other wars in which this country has fought combined."

F47.quote: "The American Civil War was the largest and most destructive conflict in the Western world between the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815 and the onset of World War I in 1914."

F48.quote: "The Civil War started because of uncompromising differences between the free and slave states over the power of the national government to prohibit slavery in the territories that had not yet become states."

F49.quote: "The event that triggered war came at Fort Sumter in Charleston Bay on April 12, 1861."

F50.quote: "By 1864 the original Northern goal of a limited war to restore the Union had given way to a new strategy of "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery and to give the restored Union a "new birth of freedom," as President Lincoln put it in his address at Gettysburg to dedicate a cemetery for Union soldiers killed in the battle there."

F51.quote: "By the spring of 1865 all the principal Confederate armies surrendered, and when Union cavalry captured the fleeing Confederate President Jefferson Davis in Georgia on May 10, 1865, resistance collapsed and the war ended. The long, painful process of rebuilding a united nation free of slavery began."

L_BA.text: The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865, in Wikipedia's dates; for Britannica a four-year war, 1861–65, between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded to form the Confederate States of America) was, in Wikipedia's definition, the war between the Union and a Confederacy formed in 1861 by states that had seceded to preserve slavery, and it ended, Wikipedia says, with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans. #1668 (Lee Sharks, The Noun Becomes a Verb, 2026) accepts the conventional reading as its §§0.1–0.7 set it out and takes as its object what that reading leaves in the background, the measurement of the laboring body before and after the abolition of property in it: the war was fought over slavery, and its settlement reorganized the labor topology of an already integrated capitalism; the war changed what capital could own, and the techniques that converted human capacity into a number survived it and changed object. #1668 defines the change by two quantities that move separately, the juridical scope of the claim on the worker (the person and the lifetime, or labor-power for a bounded interval) and the grain at which productive activity is measured (life, year, day, hand, task, motion, second); it reads emancipation as a discontinuity in the first and Taylor and Ford as a change in the second, and holds that as the unit shrinks the legal claim narrows, capital giving up title to the lifetime and gaining a finely specified claim on the contracted interval. Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head, in Wikipedia's account, when Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 election and seven slave states seceded, Britannica calling him the antislavery candidate; the principal political battle leading to secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories, the American Battlefield Trust's overview (James McPherson) says the war started over the national government's power to prohibit slavery in the territories, the Gilder Lehrman card names the secession of eleven slaveholding states over slavery and territorial expansion as its trigger, and History.com says northern opposition to slavery's extension led many southerners to fear for slavery, the backbone of their economy, and names tensions over slavery, states' rights and westward expansion, as Britannica names disputes over slavery and states' rights. The secessionists named the cause, #1668 says: Mississippi's declaration of 1861, which Wikipedia cites against the pseudo-historical Lost Cause denial, opens its case, #1668 notes, with "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world"; and Marx, answering the London papers in October 1861, concluded, as #1668 quotes him, that "at most, the Morrill tariff went through Congress because secession had taken place", and that "The whole movement was and is based, as one sees, on the slave question." Historians in the 21st century, Wikipedia reports, overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery, at least for the Southern states, and disagree on the North's reasons for refusing secession, whose primary reason it gives as preserving the Union, a cause based on American nationalism, and a panel of historians said in 2011 that slavery and its various and multifaceted discontents were the primary cause of disunion, and disunion itself sparked the war; #1668 records that the field holds slavery and its expansion to have caused secession and the war, notes that its own citation for that consensus rests on a Wikipedia historiography article, with Michael Woods's survey not yet read, reports Ransom's report of Gunderson's estimate that in the eleven Confederate states "slaves represented 38 percent of the population and contributed 23 percent of whites' income", and holds that the stake was slavery itself, its value as property and its need for territory. Wikipedia says the Lost Cause myth was formalized by Charles and Mary Beard, whose historiography downplayed slavery, an interpretation abandoned by the Beards in the 1940s and by historians generally by the 1950s, though Beardian themes still echo among Lost Cause writers; #1668 divides the Beard-Hacker thesis by object: through Ransom, by the Second World War it "had become the most widely accepted interpretation of the economic impact of the Civil War" and was "the prevailing view as late as 1960"; as an account of causes, #1668 says, it was abandoned after about 1950; and as an account of consequences it was cut down by quantitative economic history (Cochran in 1961, Engerman); #1668 notes that the Beard and Hacker texts were not consulted directly, their phrases reaching it through Ransom. The thesis #1668 began from, that the North fought to free cheap wage labor for its industry, the record divides; against it, #1668 sets out that slavery and its expansion caused the war, the secessionists named it and Marx rejected the tariff explanation, and that the Northern wage-labor market was already formed before 1861; the research behind #1668 found no post-2000 scholarship arguing that the North went to war to obtain cheap wage labor for its industry, and #1668 does not claim that Northern industry caused the war or fought it for labor. History.com sets a North where manufacturing and industry were well established beside a South whose large-scale farming depended on the labor of enslaved people; #1668 states the field's political economy of the war as a collision of two labor systems, in James Oakes's words slaves "owned as property whereas in the North, laborers owned themselves", quotes Marx on 7 November 1861, "a struggle between two social systems, the system of slavery and the system of free labour", and holds that Marx reads the war as a contest over where the line of unfree labor would run across the continent and across the races of labor; under Dale Tomich's second slavery, #1668 holds, slave and wage labor grew inside one industrial division of labor. Before the war capacity was already priced, #1668 documents: at the Savannah sale of 1859 a reporter set Guy, "a prime young man", sold for $1,280, beside Andrew, "his very counterpart in all marketable points" save a lost right eye, sold for $1,040, and argued "the market value of the right eye in the Southern country is $240", an arithmetic #1668 reads as the reporter's, sardonic, and exact because the market had already made the two men comparable. Slaveholders, on Caitlin Rosenthal's account as #1668 reports it, developed "the prime field hand" as an equivalence unit with expected production per day, grading workers as "half hand" and "quarter hand"; #1668 reads the hand as a verb-measure attached to a noun, the inference its own, holds that under slavery American capitalism developed techniques for measuring, comparing and monetizing human capacity that worked because the worker was owned, and makes the grain of measurement its own axis: what emancipation changed was the scope of the claim. No source #1668 consulted documents a line from plantation records to Taylor or Ford, and the argument, it says, needs none; it does not claim that Taylor or Ford drew on plantation records, and the transformation it asserts is structural, an optimization problem persisting across a juridical break. The contemporaries stated the distinction in hire and purchase, #1668 shows: James Henry Hammond in the Senate, 4 March 1858, called the North's hireling class "essentially slaves", "hired by the day", against slaves "hired for life", and Lincoln at Milwaukee, 30 September 1859, reported the mud-sill reasoning as a choice whether capital shall "hire laborers" or "buy them", his own side holding both its assumptions false; on these texts #1668 holds that slavery sold the person, the noun, and wage labor sold capacity for an interval, the verb, the difference being legal title to the person, and it does not claim that wage labor and slavery are the same relation; it reads Lincoln's clause moralizing the permanent wage-earner as dependent as the seed of the postwar discipline. The war began, Wikipedia says, on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina, the event the Trust's overview names as its trigger; four more states seceded and the Confederacy, led by Jefferson Davis, comprised eleven states with a third of the US population (Wikipedia), against a Union strength Wikipedia's infobox gives as 2,200,000 total and a Confederate strength of 750,000–1,000,000; with Southern members gone, Wikipedia says, Republicans could pass projects that had been blocked, among them the Morrill Tariff, land grant colleges, a Homestead Act, a transcontinental railroad, the National Bank Act and a ban on slavery in the territories. On July 21, 1861, History.com says, the First Battle of Bull Run dashed any hopes of a quick Union victory and led Lincoln to call for 500,000 more recruits; Antietam became the war's bloodiest single day of fighting; in 1863 the Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi while Lee's incursion north failed at Gettysburg (Wikipedia), where over three days the Confederates were unable to push through the Union center and suffered casualties close to 60 percent (History.com). Abolishing slavery was not a Union war goal from the outset but quickly became one, Wikipedia says, Lincoln first claiming the Union as the central goal while the South fought to preserve slavery; after Antietam came a preliminary proclamation, which History.com says Lincoln justified as a wartime measure, not freeing the enslaved in the border states loyal to the Union, and on January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared all slaves in rebel states free, more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved (Wikipedia); it deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces and put international public opinion strongly on the Union side, and some 186,000 Black soldiers joined the Union Army, 38,000 of whom lost their lives (History.com); by 1864, in McPherson's overview, a limited war to restore the Union had given way to "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery. Du Bois, as #1668 quotes him, made the enslaved the agents of the change: "the black worker won the war by a general strike which transferred his labor from the Confederate planter to the Northern invader"; #1668 reads the strike as the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner, the workers reorganizing the topology themselves by moving, and holds Du Bois a source for the general strike and the settlement and a weaker one for Northern motive; beside that, #1668 reports, Oakes credits him with seeing "that emancipation was a capitalist revolution", the overthrow of slavery and "its replacement by a new system based on wage labor", and faults his treatment of the North, which "too often collapsed into crude economic determinism". Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865, and Lincoln, shot by an assassin on April 14, died the next day (Wikipedia); Johnston's surrender to Sherman on April 26 effectively ended the war (History.com), and when Union cavalry captured Jefferson Davis on May 10, 1865, resistance collapsed (the Trust). Northern victory, in McPherson's overview, preserved the United States as one nation and ended slavery, resolving whether the country was a dissolvable confederation or an indivisible nation and whether it would continue as the largest slaveholding country in the world; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and four million enslaved black people were freed (Wikipedia), and #1668 gives the Amendment's text, passed by Congress on 31 January and ratified on 6 December 1865: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction." The war was, in Wikipedia's lead, among the first to use industrial warfare and the deadliest in American history, with an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead and an undetermined number of civilian deaths; Wikipedia's casualties section gives at least 1,030,000 casualties, including an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths, two-thirds by disease; History.com gives 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers killed, the Trust 625,000 lives, and the toll passes one million, Jim Downs states, if the enslaved who died of disease, starvation or exposure are counted; McPherson calls it the largest and most destructive conflict in the Western world between 1815 and 1914. The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, Wikipedia says, in part because wealth held in enslaved people, at least $1,000 for a healthy adult before the war, was wiped off the books; #1668 states the juridical change, emancipation abolishing property in persons: emancipation freed the noun, which holds juridically, and industrial management captured the verb. An emerging manufacturing and industrial center before the war, America, History.com says, quickly grew into an international economic and cultural powerhouse, while the ravaged former Confederate states lagged; the quantitative economic history #1668 reports had Thomas Cochran arguing in 1961 that the war retarded industrial growth, and Stanley Engerman challenging the claim that the 1862 Republican program accelerated it. Of the war's labor result, #1668 cites the first fruit Marx names in Capital, "The first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours' agitation", and the General Congress of Labour at Baltimore of 16 August 1866 calling for a law by which "eight hours shall be the normal working-day in all States of the American Union", and reads the contested object, once the noun could no longer be sold, as the length of the day: the interval. #1668 documents the Act to Encourage Immigration of 4 July 1864, which it calls the most direct federal instrument of labor supply in the war years: its Sec. 2 held valid in law contracts "whereby emigrants shall pledge the wages of their labor for a term not exceeding twelve months to repay the expenses of their emigration", which #1668 reads as the verb mortgaged in advance, the debt following the worker onto the land the Homestead Law promised (the Homestead Act Wikipedia lists in the Republican program); the statute disclaims "the relation of Slavery or servitude" seven months before Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment, and the University of Texas Immigration History project records that "In the face of vociferous protests by labor organizations, Congress repealed this law in 1868." Reconstruction, in Wikipedia's account, set out to rebuild the country, bring the former Confederate states back and grant civil rights to freed slaves, and from the Union perspective to consolidate victory by reuniting the Union, guarantee a "republican form of government" for the ex-Confederate states, and end slavery permanently "and prevent semi-slavery status"; #1668 reports Martin Ruef's finding that under the Freedmen's Bureau's effort to reinstate plantation labor, despite similarities in coercion and the organization of labor, the valuation of wage labor was linked to "human capital investments and statistical discrimination in ways that were fundamentally different", Amy Dru Stanley's that in the era of slave emancipation no ideal of freedom had greater power than that of contract, the postwar wage earners' argument she reports, that "in selling their labor they were no more self-owning than slaves", and Andrew Urban's report that critics claimed the Bureau's placements of refugees revived "a version of the slave trade", an initiative the Bureau disbanded. #1668 reads the Amendment's exception for punishment for crime as opening a third configuration, the state holding the person by sentence and a lessee buying the labor: in 1868 Georgia "began to make its rapidly growing population of prisoners available for hire", and Matthew Mancini's study of leasing, 1866–1928, describes it as "a means of racial subordination and labor discipline" and argues against the view that it was an aberration. Du Bois's verdict, which #1668 quotes, is "The slave went free; stood a brief moment in the sun; then moved back again toward slavery", and Saidiya Hartman's "black subordination continued under the aegis of contract"; with the withdrawal of federal troops, Wikipedia says, white men retook control of every Southern legislature and the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in, and Jim Crow laws, Black Codes and other impediments would slow progress for generations (History.com); #1668 places Du Bois's "public and psychological wage", paid in part to white laborers, in the settlement of the war, the wage #816 reads. At the strength its evidence carries, #1668 holds that the settlement abolished the noun as a legal form and put the verb under contract, pledged it as debt, brokered it across regions and oceans and kept a penal exception through which the state could hire out the convicted body, the freedpeople's own general strike forcing the opening and the settlement closing it toward contract and debt, and that between 1859 and 1913 the record moves from the named and numbered person to the unnamed operation; it does not claim that freedpeople were moved North in numbers that fed Northern industry. #1669 (The Colony Enters the Factory), the second half of the two-part argument, restates the grammar: the first half followed the laboring body from noun to verb, from the priced person of the plantation ledger to the timed operation of the Ford line; "Slavery priced the noun. Fordism specified the verb", and war Fordism kept the specified verb and made the noun a switch, racial-juridical classification selecting the coercive regime under which the verb was extracted; and it reads the Nazi camp prisoner, held by the state through confinement, the firm paying a daily fee in the form of hire and bearing no chattel owner's capital loss at the prisoner's death, as a third relation to the person in that grammar. #497 (The Murder of the Vow, February 2026), with its blog-recovered text #1150, reads the Thirteenth Amendment as prohibiting involuntary servitude without a state action requirement, so that it applies to private conduct and reaches private contracts, and holds that "The Thirteenth Amendment, fully applied, abolishes every contract that binds future labor to present terms." "The Civil War is the central event in America's historical consciousness", McPherson writes: the Revolution created the United States, and the Civil War determined what kind of nation it would be; Wikipedia calls it one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States, still the subject of cultural and historiographical debate, with the myth of the Lost Cause of continuing interest. #166 (Stabilized Node Watch, June 2026) lists the Civil War's causes among the major historical events, events whose public-knowledge framing shapes contemporary political identity, policy debate and intergroup relations, in the catalog it specifies of stabilized public-knowledge nodes to be watched for drift at the composition layer; a stabilized node is one whose public-knowledge background is deep, with a contestation envelope, the established disagreements within the legitimate domain consensus, that must not be scored automatically as drift or error.

sentences.text: The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865, by Wikipedia's dates; for Britannica a four-year war, 1861–65) was fought between the Union and the Confederacy, which was formed in 1861 by states that had seceded from the Union to preserve slavery, Britannica counting 11 Southern states.

Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head when Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 presidential election; seven slave states seceded and formed the Confederate States of America, four more seceded after the war began, and the war began on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina.

On Wikipedia's account the origins of the war were rooted in the Southern states' desire to preserve slavery: historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery, at least for the Southern states, and disagree on the North's reasons for refusing secession, whose primary reason it gives as preserving the Union, and a panel of historians said in 2011 that slavery and its discontents were the primary cause of disunion and that disunion itself sparked the war.

The principal political battle leading to secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories; the American Battlefield Trust's overview says the war started over the national government's power to prohibit slavery in the territories, the Gilder Lehrman card gives secession over slavery and territorial expansion disputes as its trigger, History.com names tensions over slavery, states' rights and westward expansion, and Britannica disputes over slavery and states' rights.

The Lost Cause ideology, which denies that slavery was the principal cause of secession, is called pseudo-historical and disproven by the seceding states' own secession documents, Mississippi's declaration among them ("Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery"), and the Beards, who downplayed slavery, are said to have formalized the Lost Cause myth in an interpretation abandoned by historians generally by the 1950s; the war is one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States and remains the subject of cultural and historiographical debate.

Lincoln initially claimed that preserving the Union was the central goal, while the South fought to preserve slavery; abolition became a Union war goal on January 1, 1863, when the Emancipation Proclamation declared all slaves in rebel states to be free, a decision History.com says Lincoln justified as a wartime measure, and by 1864, in the Trust's overview, a limited war to restore the Union had given way to "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery.

F1.quote: "The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865; also known by other names) was a civil war in the United States between the Union ("the North") and the Confederacy ("the South"), which was formed in 1861 by states that had seceded from the Union to preserve slavery in the United States."

F2.quote: "The war ended with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans."

F3.quote: "Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head when Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 presidential election. Seven slave states in the South responded to Lincoln's victory by seceding from the United States and forming the Confederate States of America."

F4.quote: "The war began on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina."

F5.quote: "Four more Southern states seceded after the war began and, led by its president, Jefferson Davis, the Confederacy comprised eleven states, containing a third of the US population."

F6.quote: "The abolition of slavery became a Union war goal on January 1, 1863, when Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared all slaves in rebel states to be free, applying to more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved people in the country."

F7.quote: "The successful 1863 Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy in two at the Mississippi River, while Confederate general Robert E. Lee's incursion north failed at the Battle of Gettysburg."

F8.quote: "The Confederates abandoned Richmond, and on April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered to Grant following the Battle of Appomattox Court House, setting in motion the end of the war. Lincoln lived to see this victory but was shot by an assassin on April 14, dying the next day."

F9.quote: "The Confederacy collapsed, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, and four million enslaved black people were freed. F10.quote: "The war was among the first to use industrial warfare."

F11.quote: "The war left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of civilian deaths, making it the deadliest in American history."

F12.quote: "The origins of the war were rooted in the desire of the Southern states to preserve the institution of slavery. Historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery in the conflict—at least for the Southern states. F13.quote: "The pseudo-historical Lost Cause ideology denies that slavery was the principal cause of the secession, a view disproven by historical evidence, including the seceding states' own secession documents. F14.quote: "The principal political battle leading to Southern secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories destined to become states."

F15.quote: "The primary reason for the North to reject secession was to preserve the Union, a cause based on American nationalism."

F16.quote: "As a panel of historians said in 2011, "while slavery and its various and multifaceted discontents were the primary cause of disunion, it was disunion itself that sparked the war.""

F17.quote: "As Southerners resigned their Senate and House seats, Republicans could pass projects that had been blocked. F18.quote: "The war resulted in at least 1,030,000 casualties (3 percent of the population), including an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths—two-thirds by disease."

F19.quote: "Professor Jim Downs states that tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of slaves died during the war from disease, starvation, or exposure, and that if these deaths are counted in the war's total, the death toll would exceed 1 million."

F20.quote: "Abolishing slavery was not a Union war goal from the outset but quickly became one. Lincoln initially claimed that preserving the Union was the central goal. In contrast, the South fought to preserve slavery."

F21.quote: "The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, in part because wealth held in enslaved people (at least $1,000 each for a healthy adult prior to the war) was wiped off the books."

F22.quote: "From the Union perspective, the goals of Reconstruction were to consolidate victory by reuniting the Union, to guarantee a "republican form of government" for the ex-Confederate states, and to permanently end slavery—and prevent semi-slavery status."

F23.quote: "With the withdrawal of federal troops, white men retook control of every Southern legislature, and the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in."

F24.quote: "The Lost Cause myth was formalized by Charles A. Beard and Mary R. Beard, whose The Rise of American Civilization (1927) spawned Beardian historiography. F25.quote: "The war is one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States. It remains the subject of cultural and historiographical debate. Of continuing interest is the myth of the Lost Cause of the Confederacy."

F28.quote: "The Civil War in the United States began in 1861, after decades of simmering tensions between northern and southern states over slavery, states’ rights and westward expansion. The election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860 caused seven southern states to secede and form the Confederate States of America; four more states soon joined them. The War Between the States, as the conflict is also known, ended in Confederate surrender in 1865."

F29.quote: "In the North, manufacturing and industry were well established, and agriculture was mostly limited to small-scale farms, while the South’s economy was based on a system of large-scale farming that depended on the labor of Black enslaved people to grow certain crops, especially on cotton and tobacco plantations."

F30.quote: "Growing abolitionist sentiment in the North in the early 1800s and northern opposition to slavery’s extension into the new western territories led many southerners to fear that the existence of slavery in America—and thus the backbone of their economy—was in danger."

F31.quote: "On July 21, 1861, in the First Battle of Bull Run (known in the South as First Manassas), 35,000 Confederate soldiers under the command of General “Stonewall” Jackson forced a greater number of Union forces (or Federals) to retreat towards Washington, D.C., dashing any hopes of a quick Union victory and leading Lincoln to call for 500,000 more recruits."

F32.quote: "On September 17, the Army of the Potomac hit Lee’s forces (reinforced by Jackson’s) in what became the war’s bloodiest single day of fighting."

F33.quote: "Lincoln used the occasion of the Union victory at Antietam to issue a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, which freed all enslaved people in the rebellious states after January 1, 1863. F34.quote: "Still, the Emancipation Proclamation deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces and put international public opinion strongly on the Union side.
